docs.title: 0.1. Welcome!
docs.text:
Welcome to the manual for the variant calling course at Natural History Museum, London (September, 2026). Here, you'll find all the exercises for our two modules - Reads-to-SNPs (≈ day 1 of the course) and Basic analyses (≈ day 2). The manual will always be available to you as a future point of reference.

Learning objectives

By the end of this course you will be familar with:

  • The major steps of variant-centred analyses such as quality control, alignment, calling and filtering.
  • Standard file formats in bioinformatics such as FASTQ, SAM and VCF
  • SEAN TO ADD

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
We suggest that you take notes throughout the course, for which provide a Markdown template. To render Markdown, you can edit it in RStudio or VS Code. Alternatively, you can open the document in a code editor with Bash syntax highlighting, or even treat it as a plain text file.

Instead of copying-pasting, try retyping and annotating at least some of the commands yourself. There is as this is the surest way to learn!

docs.title: 1.1. Read QC & trimming
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this worksheet, you will:

  • Understand FASTQ file format and how it relates to the sequencing procedure.
  • Perform read quality control and trimming.
  • Become more acquainted with the Unix command line.
  • Process multiple samples with loops and package your work in a shell script.

docs.title: (1.1.1) Sequencing-by-synthesis recap
docs.text:
Sequencing by synthesis (SBS) is the core of Illumina technology. While the chemical details do not matter for our purposes, a conceptual understanding helps interpret the files passed over from a sequencing facility. The main stages of a paired-end SBS procedure can be summarised as follows:

  1. Library prep - the DNA is sheared into fragments of target length, typically a few hundred base pairs. Different adapter sequences are then ligated to the two ends of each fragment (now called an 'insert'). Each adapter contains a flow-cell binding site and a sequencing primer.
  2. Cluster generation / bridge amplification - The flow cell is a glass slide with lanes. DNA molecules bind to oligonucleotides (or 'oligos') tethered to the lane, bend over to bind a neighbouring oligo, and are copied. Repeated, this turns every molecule into a cluster of hundreds of identical copies.
  3. Sequencing - Starting from the first type of sequencing primer, fluorescent nucleotides are incorporated one per cycle. Every cycle, the flow cell is imaged, and the colour of each cluster is read off. After a given number of cycles (say, 150), the forward reads are complete. The templates are then flipped over, and the whole procedure is repeated from the 2nd sequencing primer to obtain reverse reads.

Together, these 3 videos from Illumina will hopefully make it quite clear: video 1, video 2, video 3 (watch later).

docs.title: (1.1.2) Orientation
docs.text:
Having connected to the remote machine, let's locate ourselves - where are we? You should start today's work in your home directory, so let's verify you're in the right place:

# This should print /home/userX, where X is your user ID
pwd # stands for 'print working directory'

# If you're not there:
cd ~ # equivalent to cd /home/userX, where X is your user ID

# Double-check your home directory
echo $HOME

Note that, by default, the HOME environment variable stores the path to your home directory. Inside it, we can create a directory (=folder) for today's project...

mkdir ./reads2snps

...and move inside it!

cd ./reads2snps

From now on, most commands of the Reads-to-SNPs module will assume that we are inside the ${HOME}/reads2snps directory. This means that, rather than the full path (e.g., /home/user1/reads2snps/your-directory), the commands will invoke relative paths (e.g., ./your-directory).

docs.title: (1.1.3) Back from the sequencing facility
docs.text:
Let's start by viewing the contents of /home/Share/reads2snps/original_files, a directory that stores the data we're going to work with in this module:

ls /home/Share/reads2snps/original_files

You should see multiple sub-directories with slightly cryptic names. These names are actually sample codes, and each subdirectory holds the sequencing data for an individual Littorina snail. We can peek inside one:

ls /home/Share/reads2snps/original_files/ACF_2

Inside, you should see multiple compressed FASTQ (.fastq.gz) files with compound names. This is typical for raw read data returned from a sequencing facility - in fact, the contents of the subdirectory looks almost exactly like what Sean received back in 20XX.

On original_files

Note that additional metadata files might be also given. Also note that, for the purpose of the tutorial, we have prepared subsampled versions of the original files that can be processed in seconds-to-minutes rather than hours.

For convenience, let's immediately copy over everything to your private original_files directory:

# Create private original_files
mkdir ./original_files

# Copy a directory and all its subdirectories (-r)
cp -r /home/Share/reads2snps/original_files/* ./original_files

Where the -r flag stands for 'recursive' and ensures that all the subdirectories are copied over. It is always good practice to carry on some basic checks on the integrity of a dataset. First, there should be 11 sample directories. Second, each should hold a variable, but always even, number of files. Variable - because reads sequenced on distinct lanes are packaged into separate files. Even - because each lane delivers a package of forward and reverse reads, as denoted with the _1 and _2 suffixes (look just before the format extension).

# Count subdirectories
ls ./original_files | wc -l

# Count _1 and _2 files in a few sample directories
ls ./original_files/ACF_2/*_1.fastq.gz | wc -l
ls ./original_files/ACF_2/*_2.fastq.gz | wc -l

The so-called pipe | passes the output fo the ls command to wc -l that counts the number of files. Also of note - the * symbol is a wildcard that matches all files ending in a given suffix + extension. If everything looks about right, we're ready start building our pipeline!

docs.title: (1.1.4) The FASTQ format
docs.text:
So, what kind of format is FASTQ? Developed roughly a decade after the more familiar FASTA, FASTQ was initally an ad hoc solution to the problem of keeping a sequence and its companion per-base quality values in sync. Over time, it's become the standard (see Cock et al., 2010, for an interesting historical overview).

Let's inspect one of the FASTQ files we've just copied over. We will define the sample name in an environment variable SAMPLE. This is often useful if we want to substitute the same string of characters (such as sample name) into different paths.

SAMPLE="ACF_2"

# Check the value of SAMPLE
echo $SAMPLE

# See how SAMPLE can be substituted into a path
# {} is used for clarity but is not essential
echo "./original_files/${SAMPLE}/190109_E00306_0399_AHVLYNCCXY_4_11533BR0010L01_1.fastq.gz"

The value saved in SAMPLE will persist as long as your terminal window is open, but will need to be redefined upon a reboot. Then, we can use zcat - a compression-aware variant of the standard cat Unix command for concatenating (here - just displaying) the contents of a file - piped with head, to only display the first 8 lines. 

zcat ./original_files/${SAMPLE}/190109_E00306_0399_AHVLYNCCXY_4_11533BR0010L01_1.fastq.gz | head -8

You might notice that a pattern repeats every 4 lines. This is because, in contrast to FASTA, each FASTQ sequence entry consist of 4, rather than 2, lines. These are, respectively:

  • The header that starts with a '@'. The header can have arbitrary length and store arbitrary information. Here, it consists of two main 'chunks' separated by a space. The first chunk complements the file name (specifying the instrument, flowcell, etc.), with the last two integers being the coordinates of the read's origin within the lane. These coordinates are what connects forward and reverse reads between the _1 and _2 files.
  • The sequence of bases, where 'N' stands for a base that the instrument could not call. Note that, just like in FASTA, the sequence line can be 'wrapped', i.e. split across multiple lines.
  • A '+' character or optionally a repeat of the header.
  • Phred-scaled QUAL (quality) scores. QUAL values are calculated from per-base error probabilities \(P_e\) (themselves derived from SBS colour intensities) and following the formula \(Q = -10 \log_{10} P_e\). In other words, \(Q = 0\) corresponds to a base that's definitely wrong, \(Q = 10\) corresponds to \(P_e = 0.1\), \(Q = 20\) corresponds to \(P_e = 0.01\) (1% chance of error), etc. Each QUAL value sits directly below the base it scores, so the sequence and quality lines are always the same length (and can be similarly wrapped). The scores are encoded using ASCII printable characters.

The QUAL line

Only ASCII characters from 33 onwards are used to encode QUAL scores. Note that @ and + are used to both encode QUAL scores and to demark the 1st (header) and 3rd lines, respectively. While the ASCII solution already provides a file-size advantage, modern Illumina technologies apply score-binning strategies. For example, NovaSeq 6000 uses scores of 12, 23 and 37 (-, 8 and F), plus a null score (#, or 2) for no-calls.

Another QUAL-related issue to keep in mind is the 'lossy' compression of FASTQ files downloaded from public repositories. For example, files deposited on SRA (Sequence Read Archive) - or on its ENA (European Nucleotide Archive) mirror - may be served in the SRA Lite format, which effectively erases QUAL scores. If QUAL scores matter for your analysis (as they often do), explore solutions for downloading the original, unspoiled FASTQs.

There's one more task remaining before we feed our FASTQs to bioinfomatic software, and it allows us to emphasise an important point. FASTQ files are essentially text files. The task is to combine all the _1 and _2 files into total reverse and forward read files, respectively. The solution is standard for text files - use concatenation.

As prep, let's create a directory to store the concatenated files:

mkdir ./0.raw

Note that the directory name starts with 0, which is just an index to keep track of subsequent processing steps. In larger pipelines, this convention is particularly useful.

Then, we can perform concatentaion of all _1, and separately, all _2 files using the cat command and the handy * wildcard: 

cat ./original_files/${SAMPLE}/*_1.fastq.gz > ./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz
cat ./original_files/${SAMPLE}/*_2.fastq.gz > ./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R2.fastq.gz

This does the job for one sample. However, you might imagine that copying-pasting the commands while redefining the SAMPLE variable each time could take some effort. Luckily, a handy pattern exists in bash (and many other languages) - a for loop.

To 'loop over' the different samples, we've prepared a newline-separated file with all the sample names. Copy it from the /home/Share/reads2snps directory:

cp /home/Share/reads2snps/samples.txt ./samples.txt

And read its contents as a bash array using the readarray command. In bash, you can think of an array as a space-separated list.

readarray -t SAMPLES < ./samples.txt

# View the array
# Here, {} is required
echo ${SAMPLES[@]}

Notice how viewing the array requires additional 'unpacking' of individual values using [@]. Finally, we can loop over the sample names, performing our desired concatenation:

for SAMPLE in ${SAMPLES[@]}; do
    cat ./original_files/${SAMPLE}/*_1.fastq.gz > ./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz
    cat ./original_files/${SAMPLE}/*_2.fastq.gz > ./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R2.fastq.gz
    echo "Finished sample ${SAMPLE}."
done

Note the characteristic for-loop keywords: for, do and done. While the indentation of contents (here, the two cat + echo line) is not mandatory in bash loops, it does look more legible (and pretty) this way.

In general, with a little Unix magic, we can do pretty much anything with FASTQ files. This includes relatively simple stuff, like counting the number of reads in a file:

echo $(( $(zcat ./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))

Or more complex stuff, like computing the average read length (you can learn more about awk here):

zcat ./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR%4==2 {sum+=length($0); n++} END {print sum/n}'

On the other hand, specialised suites of software exist to do exactly these operation for us. Here, we get some useful info on all our FASTQ files at once using seqkit. To use this you will need to make sure you have activated the conda environment for the course.

seqkit stats ./0.raw/*.fastq.gz

The table produced by seqkit is a good diagnostic of all the files being uncorrupted - problems such as files truncation would be indicated by diffent numbers of reads in reverse / forward files (or a failure of the seqkit command).

docs.title: (1.1.5) Quality control
docs.text:
While important, QUAL scores are not the only source of information regarding sequence quality, with other useful clues implicit to the sequences themselves. All these source of info can be jointly assessed using reports produced by the FastQC program. Let's first run it on an example sample.

# Remember to have SAMPLE defined
SAMPLE="ACF_2"

# FastQC inputs:
RAW_FASTQ_1=./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz
RAW_FASTQ_2=./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R2.fastq.gz

# Commands:
mkdir -p ./0.raw/qc
fastqc -t 1 \
    --outdir ./0.raw/qc \
    $RAW_FASTQ_1 $RAW_FASTQ_2

Note how the arguments to fastqc are split between multiple lines using backslash (\) characters - for clarity, we will often use this way of formatting longer commands. --outdir defined the output directory to write FastQC reports; the -t flag specifies the number of threads, i.e., the number of concurrent computations. In FastQC, threads translate, more simply, to the number of input files that are processed in parallel.

Multi-threading

Most bioinformatic programs can split their work across multiple threads, cutting runtime roughly in proportion to the number you give them. We stick to -t 1 throughout, since our files are small. On a real dataset, you would use as many threads as your machine provides.

After FastQC finished processing both inputs, check ./0.raw/qc with ls - you should be able to find two HTML reports. Using a command (e.g., scp -i cX.pem userX@ip-address:/home/userX/read2snps/0.raw/qc/*.html . run from your local machine), Filezilla or another method, download the reports to your local machine. Both reports should look very encouraging, indicating no issues with the read data. For a contrast, you can see an example of a bad FastQC report here.

docs.title: (1.1.5) Adapter trimming & filtering
docs.text:
Even with high-quality read data, there are still good reasons to trim our reads. Individual reads might display various artefacts: very short inserts (in low-input libraries, adapters can even ligate to each other, producing insert-free adapter dimers) or a steeper-than-average drop-off in base quality, to name a few. For the trimming task, we will use fastp - Trimmomatic is one popular alternative.

Again, let's use the example sample to demonstrate running fastp:

# Remember to have SAMPLE defined
SAMPLE="ACF_2"

# fastp inputs:
RAW_FASTQ_1=./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz
RAW_FASTQ_2=./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R2.fastq.gz

# fastp outputs:
TRIMMED_FASTQ_1=./1.trimmed/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz
TRIMMED_FASTQ_2=./1.trimmed/${SAMPLE}_R2.fastq.gz
FASTP_HTML=./1.trimmed/qc/${SAMPLE}_fastp.html

# Commands:
mkdir -p ./1.trimmed ./1.trimmed/qc
fastp \
    -i $RAW_FASTQ_1 -I $RAW_FASTQ_2 \
    -o $TRIMMED_FASTQ_1 -O $TRIMMED_FASTQ_2 \
    --thread 1 \
    -u 40 -q 15 \
    -g -c -y -Y 30 \
    --html $FASTP_HTML \
    --report_title $SAMPLE

A few more flags here, so let's break them down:

  • -u 40 allows up to 40% of a read's bases to be 'unqualified' (see below) - above that, the whole read, and its mate, are discarded rather than trimmed. (This is on by default.)
  • -q 15 sets the QUAL score below which a base counts as 'unqualified'.
  • -g enables the trimming of poly-G tails introduced by some modern Illumina technologies (such as NextSeq or NovaSeq - not relevant here, but good to remember).
  • -c enables base correction in regions where forward and reverse reads overlap.
  • -y enables a complexity filter, with -Y 30 setting its threshold - reads with <30% base-to-base change are dropped (think of a repetitive region such as AAAAA...)
  • --html and --report_title define a fastp report that compares the properties of reads before and after trimming - take a look, if interested!

Note that fastp detects and trims a range of standard Illumina adapters by default. As a basic sanity check, it makes sense to compare the length of reads before and after trimming using seqkit stats:

seqkit stats ./0.raw/${SAMPLE}*.fastq.gz
seqkit stats ./1.trimmed/${SAMPLE}*.fastq.gz

docs.title: (1.1.6) A shell script
docs.text:
Up to now, we've been executing commands directly from the command line. That works, but once you close your terminal, the record of what you've run is gone. A shell script is simply those same commands saved in a file, so the whole analysis can be rerun in one go — and the file itself becomes a permanent record of what you did.

We now have everything we need: FastQC and fastp commands that work on one sample, and an understanding of how a for loop can be used to iterate over all samples. Let's put everything together. We suggest that you initially open a new local file and call it run_qc_trim.sh, where the .sh extension identifies a shell script.

The first line of a script is the shebang, which defines bash as the interpreter for our script:

#!/bin/bash

By default, bash carries on after an error, so a script can fail at step 1 and keep running. The next line prevents this behaviour (by terminating the run upon any error) and will save you lots of debugging in the future:

set -euo pipefail

Our script needs to know which samples to process. Rather than hard-coding the file name, we read it from the first argument given on the command line. This is available as $1:

IN_FILE=$1
readarray -t SAMPLES < "$IN_FILE"

Now, to make our script self-sufficient, we want it to create all its output directories. mkdir normally throws an error if the requested directory exists, but this is prevented by the -p flag:

mkdir -p ./0.raw ./1.trimmed ./0.raw/qc ./1.trimmed/qc

Then the loop itself. To avoid rewriting the FastQC and fastp commands, let's make it define all inputs / outputs as variables...

# Start of loop
for SAMPLE in ${SAMPLES[@]}; do
    echo "Processing sample ${SAMPLE}..."

    RAW_FASTQ_1=./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz
    RAW_FASTQ_2=./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R2.fastq.gz
    TRIMMED_FASTQ_1=./1.trimmed/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz
    TRIMMED_FASTQ_2=./1.trimmed/${SAMPLE}_R2.fastq.gz
    FASTP_HTML=./1.trimmed/qc/${SAMPLE}_fastp.html

...and finally the two commands, copied straight from the previous sections:

    fastqc -t 1 \
        --outdir ./0.raw/qc \
        $RAW_FASTQ_1 $RAW_FASTQ_2

    fastp \
        -i $RAW_FASTQ_1 -I $RAW_FASTQ_2 \
        -o $TRIMMED_FASTQ_1 -O $TRIMMED_FASTQ_2 \
        --thread 1 \
        -u 40 -q 15 \
        -g -c -y -Y 30 \
        --html $FASTP_HTML \
        --report_title $SAMPLE

    echo "Finished sample ${SAMPLE}."
done
# End of loop

Your script is ready! You should now transfer it to your reads2snps directory. One last step: a text file is not executable by default, so we need to grant it permission to run:

chmod +x run_qc_trim.sh

And run it, passing the sample list as the argument:

./run_qc_trim.sh samples.txt

You can find the whole script in the box below.

The complete script 
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Run as: ./run_qc_trim.sh samples.txt

# Samples are read from a file, one name per line.
IN_FILE=$1
readarray -t SAMPLES < "$IN_FILE"

mkdir -p ./0.raw ./1.trimmed ./0.raw/qc ./1.trimmed/qc

for SAMPLE in ${SAMPLES[@]}; do
    echo "Processing sample ${SAMPLE}..."

    RAW_FASTQ_1=./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz
    RAW_FASTQ_2=./0.raw/${SAMPLE}_R2.fastq.gz
    TRIMMED_FASTQ_1=./1.trimmed/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz
    TRIMMED_FASTQ_2=./1.trimmed/${SAMPLE}_R2.fastq.gz
    FASTP_HTML=./1.trimmed/qc/${SAMPLE}_fastp.html

    fastqc -t 1 \
        --outdir ./0.raw/qc \
        $RAW_FASTQ_1 $RAW_FASTQ_2

    fastp \
        -i $RAW_FASTQ_1 -I $RAW_FASTQ_2 \
        -o $TRIMMED_FASTQ_1 -O $TRIMMED_FASTQ_2 \
        --thread 1 \
        -u 40 -q 15 \
        -g -c -y -Y 30 \
        --html $FASTP_HTML \
        --report_title $SAMPLE

    echo "Finished sample ${SAMPLE}."
done

docs.title: 1.2. Alignment to reference
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this worksheet, you will:

  • Map reads with BWA and process the output with SAMtools.
  • Understand the structure of a SAM / BAM file.
  • Perform some basic QC on a SAM / BAM.

In this tutorial we will use the BWA-MEM algorithm from the BWA (Burrows-Wheeler Aligner) package is the most widely used short read aligner. BWA uses the Burrows-Wheeler Transform to reorganise the reference genome into an index in which any sequence can be looked up directly, rather than compared against the genome position by position. Today, we will be using BWA-MEM2, a faster incarnation of the original algorithm that produces identical alignments; even faster algorithms are on the horizon, so keep an eye for the future.

docs.title: (1.2.1) The reference
docs.text:
We do need a reference genome assembly for aligning our reads. We will download it from a public archive hosted by NCBI. As always, it's reasonable to create a new directory to store the reference:

mkdir ./ref

We're going to use the US_GU_Lsax_2.0 assembly - search for Littorina saxatilis in the NCBI genome browser or, alternatively, open this link directly. Try locating the 'FTP' button. FTP stands for File Transfer Protocol and is a convention for serving files over a network - here, it simply takes you to a plain directory listing of everything NCBI holds for this assembly. Copy the link to the file ending in _genomic.fna.gz (alternatively, we pasted it below!).

We can now download the assembly using the wget command, specifying ./ref as the target directory:

wget https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/037/325/665/GCF_037325665.1_US_GU_Lsax_2.0/GCF_037325665.1_US_GU_Lsax_2.0_genomic.fna.gz \
--directory-prefix=./ref

FASTA extensions

Note that .fa, .fasta and .fna are all acceptable extensions for FASTA files - the latter just specifies that we're dealing with nucleic acids.

As always, let's inspect the FASTA's statistics with seqkit stats:

# -N 50 appends N50 as an extra column
seqkit stats -N 50 ./ref/*

That's a decent-sized metazoan genome!! It's approximately 12 times larger than the C. elegans genome, for example, but still 2.5 times smaller than the human genome. As indicated by the N50 statistic, it's also well-assembled, with half of the assembly in pieces longer than 67.5 Mb. This is chromosome-scale.

Aligning a decent depth sample against this assembly would take a few hours. To avoid this computational burden, let's focus on the first 1 MB of the largest chromosome. Again, seqkit proves its usefulness:

# Define variables to shorten the command itself
IN_FASTA=./ref/GCF_037325665.1_US_GU_Lsax_2.0_genomic.fna.gz
OUT_FASTA=./ref/chrom1_1Mb.fa

# Some piped seqkit commands
seqkit sort -l -r $IN_FASTA | seqkit head -n 1 | seqkit subseq -r 1:1000000 > $OUT_FASTA

You can check the seqkit docs for the sort, head and subseq commands, but the overall purpose seems clear. Voilà! We've extracted our target 1 Mb. In fact, also thanks to processing with seqkit, the reads we're working with align exactly against this sequence.

How to identify the best reference for your project?

In general, you should aim for your reference assembly to be of the highest possible quality, as defined by N50 and BUSCO completeness, among other statistics. Depending on your organism and your dataset, this might be the best-assembled genome from among your sequenced samples, representing the same or a related species. On the other hand, chromosome-level (or T2T, i.e., telomere-to-telomere) assemblies are available from public repositories for many eukaryotes, making them an obvious choice. Assemblies of a very high quality are also available from the Darwin Tree of Life project.

The choice of reference assembly is far from inconsequential (see, e.g., Mohn et al., 2025), starting at the alignment stage. For example, you might imagine that reads will map better to a con-specific than to a hetero-specific reference genome.

docs.title: (1.2.2) Alignment
docs.text:
Before we can run the alignment, we need to index the reference. Indexing is a one-off procedure that writes a data structure allowing the aligner to navigate the reference quickly. It's as simple as:

REF=./ref/chrom1_1Mb.fa
bwa-mem2 index $REF

This should produce five files with unfamiliar extensions: .0123, .amb, .ann, .bwt.2bit.64 and .pac. The index files should always remain in the same directory as their parent sequence.

Now, we can run the actual alignment using BWA-MEM2. This takes the reference and (trimmed) read files as inputs and produces an alignment in the SAM format, which we discuss below.

# Remember to have SAMPLE defined
SAMPLE="ACF_2"

# BWA-MEM2 inputs:
REF=./ref/chrom1_1Mb.fa
TRIMMED_FASTQ_1=./1.trimmed/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz
TRIMMED_FASTQ_2=./1.trimmed/${SAMPLE}_R2.fastq.gz

# BWA-MEM2 outputs:
SAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.sam

# Commands:
mkdir -p ./2.aligned
bwa-mem2 mem \
    -t 1 \
    -R "@RG\tID:${SAMPLE}\tSM:${SAMPLE}\tPL:ILLUMINA\tLB:${SAMPLE}\tPU:${SAMPLE}" \
    $REF \
    $TRIMMED_FASTQ_1 \
    $TRIMMED_FASTQ_2 \
    > $SAM
Let's review the flags:

  • -t specifies the number of threads. This is normally set to be quite large (e.g., 18 or even more), since alignment tends to be relatively slow.
  • -R specifies a string of characters defining the so-called read group. The string starts with @RG, with subsequent fields separated by tabs (\t). Here, we repeat the sample ID in most fields (though it should primarily go to SM, or 'sample'), except PL ('sequencing platform'). A 'minimal' read group is essential for variant calling (to link reads with their samples of origin) and enough for our purposes, but the information could be much richer. For instance, a sample sequenced twice on different flowcells would keep one SM value but take two read groups with distinct ID ('identifier') and PU ('platform unit') values.

Note that the output SAM file is specified through > rather than a flag. BWA-MEM2 does have an output flag (-o), but writing to standard output is a common pattern. Also note how the reference and FASTQ files are provided without any flags, as positional arguments.

docs.title: (1.2.3) The SAM format
docs.text:
The SAM (Sequence Alignment/Map) format defines yet another set of conventions (described in full here) to store sequence information in a text file. But where a FASTQ record describes a read in isolation, a SAM record describes a read together with the position it was assigned in the reference. The file splits into a header and a 'body'.

Let's inspect the header first. We will use a command from the dedicated SAMtools library:

SAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.sam
samtools view -H $SAM

It is the -H flag that restricts the output to the header. Every header line starts with @ followed by a two-letter record type. You should find three kinds:

  • @SQ - one line per reference sequence, with its name (SN) and length (LN). Ours has a single @SQ line, since we aligned to one sequence only.
  • @RG - the different fields of the read group we passed to BWA-MEM2.
  • @PG - one line per command that touched the file. Two should be shown: one for BWA-MEM2 and one for samtools view. The latter is added 'on the fly' as the header is printed to screen, and is not actually part of the file.

Now - the alignments themselves. In contrast to FASTQ, there's a one-to-one correspondence between SAM records and lines of the file. We can request the first two with head -2 and pipe them to less -S for convenient viewing:

# Note that samtools view omits the header by default
samtools view $SAM | head -2 | less -S

On less

In contrast to cat, less lets you navigate its input rather than letting everything scroll past non-interactively (compare the behaviour by substituting head -200 into the example above!). The -S flag stops long lines from wrapping onto the next line, so each record stays on one row. Use the arrow keys to move (up and down by line, left and right by half a screen width), and press Q to quit.

Each line consists of 11 mandatory tab-separated fields, followed by optional ones. The meaning of mandatory fields is fixed by position, and below we highlight some of the key ones (see the specs for a full breakdown):

  • Field 2 - FLAG. An integer encoding a set of yes/no properties, each a power of two, summed together. The individual attributes are encoded by smaller integers (or bits), so any combination of them sums to a unique total. You can use samtools flags to decode it. For example, samtools flags 99 returns PAIRED,PROPER_PAIR,MREVERSE,READ1, i.e. bits 1, 2, 32 and 64. In human terms, we learn that the read is paired-end (bit 1) and that both mates are properly aligned (bit 2). See section 1.4 of the specs for the full list.
  • Fields 3 + 4 - RNAME + POS. These constitute the alignment itself, specifying the reference sequence (in a real setting - one out of many chromosomes or assembly contigs) and the position of the leftmost aligned base. RNAME must match one of the @SQ names from the header.
  • Field 5 - MAPQ. The mapping quality - a Phred-scaled measure of confidence that the read belongs here rather than anywhere else. Note that this is a different quantity from the FASTQ QUAL scores, which describe base calls rather than placement - a read can consist of perfectly-called bases and still be impossible to place. We will meet MAPQ again in worksheet 1.4, where the MQ annotation we filter on is its per-site average.

Uncompressed SAM files tend to get quite big. Luckily, we can easily compress them into a binary BAM format using SAMtools:

# Specify the input SAM and output BAM
SAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.sam
BAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.bam

samtools view -b $SAM > $BAM

Where -b specifies the output format as BAM. Note that samtools view could be connected with a pipe directly to bwa-mem2 mem, avoiding the generation of a SAM intermediate altogether.

Finally, let's see how much space we've saved through compression:

# -l lists one file per line, with details
# -h prints sizes in human-readable units
ls -lh $SAM $BAM

# We don't need the SAM anymore
rm $SAM

The BAM takes up nearly four times less space - well worth it.

SAM compression

Different levels of output compression can be specified with samtools view (--output-fmt-option level=INT, from 1 to 9), but higher compression comes at the cost of longer processing time. With small files, the default level 6 is reasonable. The CRAM format compresses even further (9 MB here), but it can only be read if the reference is also provided.

docs.title: (1.2.4) Marking duplicates
docs.text:
Additional processing is required to make sure our BAM is fit for variant calling. One artefact that becomes apparent after alignment is read duplication, when multiple read pairs map to the same position. Depending on the mechanism, two types of duplicates are distinguished: optical and PCR. Optical duplicates arise during imaging, when a single cluster on the flow cell is read as two adjacent ones. PCR duplicates arise earlier, during library preparation, when amplification produces several copies of one fragment.

Below, we follow the recommended procedure for duplicate marking. This requires some pre-processing of the BAMs:

# Define input and output;
# 'tmp' stands for 'temporary'
IN_BAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.bam
OUT_BAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.tmp.bam

# A few commands...
samtools collate -@ 1 -O $IN_BAM |\
samtools fixmate -@ 1 -m - - |\
samtools sort -@ 1 -o $OUT_BAM -
The three SAMtools commands are piped together, and the - function as placeholders for inputs (fixmate) and outputs. @ specifies threads. Now, the commands themselves:

  • collate groups reads of the same name together (read from field 1 of the SAM / BAM), so that both mates of a pair sit side by side in the file.
  • fixmate writes into each read's record a summary of the other read of its pair. Some (but not all) of this information is already present in fields 7-9 of the SAM / BAM. The -m flag in particular specifies adding a 'mate score' - a sum of the mate's base qualities.
  • sort sorts the file according to reference coordinates, as expected by downstream tools.

We're now ready to actually mark the duplicates: 

# We return to the original BAM name
IN_BAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.tmp.bam
OUT_BAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.bam

samtools markdup -@ 1 -d 100 $IN_BAM $OUT_BAM
rm $IN_BAM

Again, -@ specifies the threads. -d 100 is more interesting as it sets the optical duplicate distance - the distance on the flow cell within which two identical reads are called optical rather than PCR duplicates. According to the SAMtools docs, a distance of 100 units is recommended for HiSeq-style platforms (2500 for NovaSeq).

Crucially, duplicates are marked, not removed. The information is encoded in the FLAG (2nd) field of the SAM / BAM (to be precise - its value is incremented by 1024) and is later read by downstream tools such as variant callers. How many duplicates have been marked? We can count by 'fishing' for the tags added by samtools markdup using the grep Unix command:

# Make sure the variable points at the final file
BAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.bam

# Count all reads 
samtools view -c $BAM

# Count all duplicates
samtools view -c -f 1024 $BAM

# Count optical duplicate tags
samtools view $BAM | grep -c 'dt:Z:SQ' 

# Count PCR duplicate tags
samtools view $BAM | grep -c 'dt:Z:LB'

In the ACF_2 sample, it appears that PCR duplicates are way more common!

docs.title: (1.2.6) BAM QC
docs.text:
Some final sanity checks before we move on. SAMtools provides several options to collect useful statistics on our alignment. Probably the single most informative report comes from samtools flagstat which, as you might have guessed, uses the FLAG field of the file:

BAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.bam
# The report will go to a new subdirectory
FLAGSTAT=./2.aligned/qc/${SAMPLE}.flagstat

mkdir -p ./2.aligned/qc
samtools flagstat $BAM > $FLAGSTAT

We saved the flagstat report to disk, as you normally would, but for now let's display it with line numbering for ease of orientation:

# -n adds line numbers
cat -n $FLAGSTAT

Every line is a count of reads carrying a particular combination of FLAG bits (ignore the + 0 part, as the bit it counts is reportedly never set by Illumina instruments). Some key results:

  • Line 5 - duplicates is the number of duplicates we've seen earlier.
  • Line 8 - primary mapped is the proportion of reads that the aligner managed to place on the reference at all. This should be satisfyingly high in our example dataset, given how it was created... Across many samples in a real setting, you could be concerned if some display exceedingly low (or high) mapping rates for no apparent reason.
  • Line 12 - properly paired is a strict assessment of whether both mates not only map but also do so at an expected distance and orientation relative to each other. It should be lower than the mapping rate above.
  • Lines 15-16 - mate mapped to a different chr are 0 for a trivial reason: we just used one reference sequence. Normally, an excess of cross-chromosome pairs points at structural variation, misassembly or contamination.

What flagstat doesn't tell us is where along the reference the reads landed. A very useful overview is provided by samtools coverage with the -m flag. This draws an ASCII histogram with position on the x axis and percentage of bases covered (in bins) on the y axis:

samtools coverage -m $BAM

Alongside the plot it prints the summary statistics. In general, a rather flat histogram is a good sign, while dips or peaks indicate problems - like repeat regions or assembly gaps.

Finally, the richest information is provided by samtools stats, which reports several dozen statistics at once:

STATS=./2.aligned/qc/${SAMPLE}.stats
samtools stats $BAM > $STATS

The report is organised by two-letter section codes in the first column. SN holds the summaries; the remaining sections are whole distributions rather than single values. IS are insert sizes, RL read lengths, COV coverage, GCF/GCL GC content, and so on - each a table you could plot directly.

Let's at least inspect the SN lines. We can pull them out using grep, a Unix utility for searching lines that match a regular expression. We ask for lines that start (^) with SN:

grep "^SN" $STATS

Some important additional information include:

  • reads MQ0 shows the number of aligned reads with a mapping quality of 0. These are simply counted as mapped by flagstat.
  • error rate - is the proportion of aligned bases that differ from the reference.
  • insert size average is the average length of inserts as calculated from the alignment, while insert size standard deviation is.. the standard deviation. The latter number reveals the frequency at which the mates map at implausible distances from each other.

Collecting BAM stats

In a 'production pipeline', we would probably like to check our BAMs in bulk rather than examining one sample at a time. The MultiQC software has been designed to help with exactly this task on FASTQ and BAM files, taking FastQC, fastp and SAMtools reports as input.

docs.title: (1.2.7) Process all samples
docs.text:
Just like previously, there remain 10 samples that need to be processed in an analogous manner. Using the commands introduced above and techniques from the previous worksheet, try and write a shell script to process the remaining samples. For simplicitly, focus on the command that are essential to producing the final BAM.

Show the answer 
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Run as: ./run_align.sh samples.txt

# Samples are read from a file, one name per line.
IN_FILE=$1
readarray -t SAMPLES < "$IN_FILE"

# The reference is the same for every sample.
REF=./ref/chrom1_1Mb.fa

mkdir -p ./2.aligned ./2.aligned/qc

for SAMPLE in ${SAMPLES[@]}; do
    echo "Processing sample ${SAMPLE}..."

    TRIMMED_FASTQ_1=./1.trimmed/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz
    TRIMMED_FASTQ_2=./1.trimmed/${SAMPLE}_R2.fastq.gz
    SAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.sam
    BAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.bam
    TMP_BAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.tmp.bam
    FLAGSTAT=./2.aligned/qc/${SAMPLE}.flagstat

    bwa-mem2 mem \
        -t 1 \
        -R "@RG\tID:${SAMPLE}\tSM:${SAMPLE}\tPL:ILLUMINA\tLB:${SAMPLE}\tPU:${SAMPLE}" \
        $REF \
        $TRIMMED_FASTQ_1 \
        $TRIMMED_FASTQ_2 \
        > $SAM

    samtools view -b -o $BAM $SAM
    rm $SAM

    samtools collate -@ 1 -O $BAM |\
    samtools fixmate -@ 1 -m - - |\
    samtools sort -@ 1 -o $TMP_BAM -

    samtools markdup -@ 1 -d 100 $TMP_BAM $BAM
    rm $TMP_BAM

    samtools flagstat $BAM > $FLAGSTAT

    echo "Finished sample ${SAMPLE}."
done

docs.title: 1.3. Variant calling
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this worksheet, you will:

  • Call variants with BCFtools.
  • Understand the structure of a VCF file.
  • Interrogate VCFs with BCFtools.
  • BONUS: call variants with GATK, if there is time.

The goal of variant calling is to determine, at every position of the reference, the alleles carried by our sample individuals - or their genotypes. Unfortunately, we never observe the genotypes directly. Instead, we are forced to work with piles of aligned (short) reads: these might be misplaced, carry errors, or be too scarce to provide sufficient information for a confident genotype call. Calling is therefore a statistical endeavour.

docs.title: (1.3.1) Calling prep
docs.text:
We will use BCFtools to perform variant calling. The software uses a joint calling strategy, originally designed to accommodate for low-coverage samples (Li, 2011): a weakly supported non-reference allele in sample A gains credibility if it's also found in sample B. While many more modern variant callers exist (see box below), BCFtools has stood the test of time (Danacek, 2021; Lefouili and Nam, 2022) and can be seamlessly integrated with SAMtools to demonstrate calling principles.

Variant calling algorithms

Apart from BCFtools, several other calling algorithms, varying in their calling principles, are in common use. GATK HaplotypeCaller, for example, performs local haplotype assembly to identify variant sites (more on that in the bonus section 1.3.7) and is likely the most widely used caller in human genomics. freebayes takes a similar haplotype-based approach but with a simpler Bayesian model. Finally, DeepVariant replaces the statistical model entirely: it turns the alignment into an image-like representation and classifies genotypes with a neural network trained on 'truth sets'. Unfortunately, benchmark rankings for all of these are built almost entirely on human datsets (Kumaran et al., 2019).

As a reminder, you should still be in your private reads2snps directory. The first task in this worksheet is to prepare a list of BAM files for joint calling. We will use the sed stream editor to write their paths to a text file based on the stored sample names.

# Just a reminder!
cd ~/reads2snps

# Define input & output names
SAMPLES=./samples.txt
BAMS=./bams.txt

sed 's|.*|2.aligned/&.bam|' $SAMPLES > $BAMS
cat $BAMS

In the sed command, s|old|new| allows us to substitute whatever matches the first part with the second. The pattern .* is a regular expression that matches any character (.) repeated any number of times (*). The matched characters are then substituted instead as & inside the longer 2.aligned/&.bam strings. Neat, isn't it?

Glob alternative

Alternatively, the BAM-path file could be written with printf '%s\n' 2.aligned/*.bam > "$BAMS". Then, however, you'd need to be sure that you want to include all the BAMs in the 2.aligned directory. Today, the answer is likely 'yes', but it is generally good practice to explicitly define the inputs based on a config.

docs.title: (1.3.2) Variant calling with BCFtools
docs.text:
Variant calling with BCFtools consists of two steps: (1) mpileup, that, for each vertical 'slice' through the given alignment (i.e., site), computes genotype likelihoods (based on base qualities, read mapping qualities, etc.) and (2) call, that evaluates the most likely genotypes under the assumption of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (Danacek, 2021). The two commands can be piped together so the intermediate never touches disk, and the final output is recorded as a VCF file. Run the caller, and then we'll break the commands down.

# BCFtools mpileup / call inputs
REF=./ref/chrom1_1Mb.fa
BAMS=./bams.txt

# BCFtools mpileup / call output
VCF_PREFIX=./3.calls/bcftools/littorina

# Commands
mkdir -p ./3.calls/bcftools
bcftools mpileup \
    -a FORMAT/SP,FORMAT/DP \
    -f $REF \
    -b $BAMS \
    -Ou |
bcftools call \
    -m \
    -a FORMAT/GQ \
    -Oz \
    -o ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz

Note that we used a VCF_PREFIX variable without an extension. This will make it easier to create multiple VCF files with different extensions, and we'll see a couple in the next worksheet. Now, what do the different flags mean?

bcftools mpileup:

  • -a annotates each record with extra fields (FORMAT/SPand FORMAT/DP) that are not emitted by default. Exactly what these mean will become clear once we inspect the VCF file (see below).
  • -f and -b specify the reference FASTA and BAM-list file, respectively.
  • -Ou specifies that the output (-O) should be in an uncompressed BCF format (u). The BCF format is a binary counterpart of VCF (think of SAM -> BAM); here, it's just used inside the pipe for efficiency.

bcftools call:

  • -m selects the 'multiallelic caller' algorithm instead of an older 'consensus caller' (-c), which can detect at most one alternative allele per site. Neither of these options is default, and one of them needs to provided.
  • -a is analogous to mpileup -a but adds fields specific to the call stage. Think of the division of labour between the two commands - while mpileup handles reads, call works with genotypes. Some annotations are derived from directly from the latter (more on that later).
  • -Oz specifies a compressed VCF output, hence the .vcf.gz extension.

One commonly included option that we deliberately avoided is -v (or --variants-only) used with bcftools call. Passing -v would emit only variant sites, discarding all invariant sites, where no alternative alleles have been called. This interferes with calculating population genetic statistics such as nucleotide diversity (\(\pi\)) and divergence (\(d_{xy}\)), so we recommend you avoid this flag, if possible.

On VCF compression

Note that VCF files produced with -Oz are compressed using bgzip and not plain gzip. Keep this in mind, since bgzip-compression is required by some commands such as bcftools index.

docs.title: (1.3.3) The VCF format
docs.text:
The VCF (Variant Call Format) is defined in full here; today we'll just cover its most important aspects.

Similarly to a SAM, a VCF splits into a header and a 'body'. Since it's a tradition by now, let's examine the header first. BCFtools is used not only for calling but for manipulating VCFs generally, and it has a dedicated command for this:

bcftools head ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz | less -S

Note that all but the final displayed line start with ##. The first always states the VCF format version - here VCFv4.2 - and further down you should find the BCFtools version and the commands that produced the file. Most of the header, though, is taken up by repeated ##INFO and ##FORMAT lines. Let's examine one:

zcat ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz | grep "##INFO" | tail -1

Where tail -1 extracts the final line of the input. Notice how the ##INFO line is essentially a dictionary entry: the key MQ takes an Integer, and it means Average mapping quality.

Now, can you recall the -a flag we passed to mpileup and call? The codes we asked for there - FORMAT/SP, FORMAT/SP, FORMAT/GQ - carry the same two prefixes as encountered in the VCF header, and for good reason. INFO and FORMAT are columns of the VCF body, each gathering a set of annotations that the header defines one by one. Every annotation therefore appears in two places - declared once in the header, and then carried as a value by those records it applies to. Let's turn to the data lines to see them. We will use another useful BCFtool command:

# grep -v matches lines that DON'T contain a pattern
bcftools view ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz | grep -v '^##' | less -S

# Or the below, without column names
# bcftools view -H ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz | less -S

You can now see the data columns with their corresponding names (top line). Unfortunately, since the columns are tab-separated and vary a lot in width, the names rarely line up neatly above their values on screen. Below column names, each line corresponds to a record - a variant or an invariant site.

Here is a breakdown of the columns that define the records:

  • CHROM — the name of the reference sequence the site sits on. This matches a ##contig line in the header.
  • POS — position of the site along the reference. For indels this is the last unaffected base immediately preceding the event.
  • ID — a variant identifier. Freshly called variants are usually ..
  • REF — the reference allele: the base(s) present at this position in the reference genome.
  • ALT — the alternate allele(s) called in the data, comma-separated if there is more than one (e.g. A,T). A . means no alternate was found (invariant site).
  • QUAL — a Phred-scaled quality score for the assertion made in the ALT column. Both variant and invariant sites can carry a QUAL value, though it is occasionally ..
  • FILTER — PASS if the site passed every filter, or a semicolon-separated list of the filters it failed (each defined by a ##FILTER line). A . means no filtering has been applied yet - as is the case for our freshly called VCF.
  • INFO — annotations defined at site-level, given as a semicolon-separated list of key=value pairs (e.g. DP=65;MQ=15, etc.). Each key is defined by an ##INFO line. A given score describes the record as a whole.
  • FORMAT — annotations defined at sample-level, given as a colon-separated list of keys only. Each key is defined by a ##FORMAT line. The order of FORMAT annotations is replicated in the sample fields (see below).
  • Sample columns — one column per sample, each holding a colon-separated list consisting of a genotype and values defined by the FORMAT column. The genotypes are encoded against the REF/ALT alleles: 0 = REF, 1 = first ALT, 2 = second ALT, and so on. Accordingly, 0/0 is homozygous reference, 0/1 heterozygous, 1/1 homozygous alternate, whereas ./. is a missing genotype.

Some of the above definitions might sound somewhat abstract. The key thing to understand is the relationship between the INFO, FORMAT and sample columns, so do spend time trying to relate them to one another.

docs.title: (1.3.4) Interrogating VCFs
docs.text:
Reading a VCF with less is fine for exploration - for extracting specific information, specialised BCFtools commands come to the rescue. Sample names, for example, can be extracted using bcftools query with the -l flag:

bcftools query -l ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz

A more elaborate query command extracts specific INFO and FORMAT annotations:

bcftools query -i 'TYPE="snp"' -f '%CHROM\t%POS\t%REF\t%ALT\t%QUAL\t%INFO/DP[\t%GT:%DP]\n' ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz | head

This prints a tab-separated table, ready for further analyses in R, for example. In the above command, note the following:

  • -i 'TYPE="snp"' keeps only SNP records - assuming we are only interested in those.
  • -f reads a string that requests specific fields:
    • % marks a field. Everything else is printed to output literally: \t is a tab and \n is a new line character.
    • INFO/ before DP is required to distinguish between site-level and sample-level values; DP is represented in both INFO and FORMAT.
    • Square brackets loop over sample-level values (same order as bcftools query -l). Note the positioning of \t - it sits inside the brackets, so a tab is printed once per sample rather than once per line.

Just like SAMtools, BCFtools can print a summary report of the whole file. This will answer one fundamental question - how many, and what kind of, sites are present in our VCF?

bcftools stats ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz | less -S

Alright, that's another big report, and we're not saving this one to disk. Instead, using some of the tricks we learnt before - but now in combination with a cut command that extracts columns 3 and 4 - we can pull out just the summary numbers:

bcftools stats ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz | grep "^SN" | cut -f3,4

Now, we have a compact report: the number of records in the file, how many of them are 'no-ALTs' (= invariant sites), and a breakdown of the rest into SNPs, indels and multiallelic sites. Of course, we can request information in an even more streamlined manner. For example, just the SNP count: 

bcftools view -Hv snps ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz | wc -l

Where -H narrows down the output to just the VCF body, -v snps requests SNPs only, and wc -l counts lines. The number shoud be identical to that reported by bcftools stats!

Finally, especially with a big VCF, you could be interested in just interrogating a specific region of a specific chromosome. First, we need to index our VCF...

bcftools index ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz

...and only access our region of interest with bcftools view. This is specified with a string provided to the -r flag: 

bcftools view -H -r NC_090245.1:1-10 ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz | less -S

Where NC_090245.1 is the name of our reference and 1-10 is the target range.

The moral is - bioinformaticians who work with VCF files typically use BCFtools every day, so familiarity with the different usage patterns is very useful (that's why we are spending time on it!). The docs are definitely your friend on this adventure.

docs.title: (1.3.6) BONUS: An alternative variant calling strategy with GATK
docs.text:
You may realise that the addition of new samples would necessitate rerunning both the bcftools mpileup and call commands. While this might not seem daunting with our sample and file sizes, adding an additional sample to a realistic dataset (say, 30 full-size Littorina genomes) means redoing the whole run. So - not a trivial cost!

This issue is addressed by a calling strategy adopted by GATK (Genome Analysis ToolKit). GATK also splits calling into two steps: however, genotype likelihoods are first computed independently for each sample, with joint calling as the second step. While the first step is not obviously cheaper, it only ever has to be done once per sample. In other words, adding sample no 31 means that 30 / 31 samples have already been processed.

Another potential advantage of GATK lies in its approach to identifying variant positions in the first place. Rather than scanning a pre-computed alignment, the per-sample HaplotypeCaller performs local re-assembly of candidate (or 'active') regions and realigns reads against the re-assembled haplotypes. This strategy has been shown to be particularly effective for the discovery of indels, many of which are missed by pileup-style callers (Poplin et al., 2017).

GATK

GATK is extensively documented, with tutorials and a user forum. Note that older GATK versions also included another calling algorithm, UnifiedGenotyper, which is essentially a pileup-style caller and of significantly less interest than HaplotypeCaller.

We have pre-computed all the gVCFs, which you can find under /home/Share/reads2snps/3.calls/gatk. For practice, run the algorithm on one sample using the commands below.

First, GATK needs one additional indexing of the reference and the BAM:

REF=./ref/chrom1_1Mb.fa
samtools dict $REF -o ${REF%.fa}.dict

# Check what % does
echo ${REF%.fa}

SAMPLE=ACF_2
BAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.bam
samtools index $BAM

Run HaplotypeCaller for one sample:

# HaplotypeCaller inputs
SAMPLE=ACF_2
BAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.bam

# HaplotypeCaller outputs
GVCF_DIR=./3.calls/gatk

# Commands
mkdir -p $GVCF_DIR
gatk HaplotypeCaller \
    --java-options "-Xmx4000m" \
    -R $REF \
    -I $BAM \
    -O ${GVCF_DIR}/${SAMPLE}.g.vcf.gz \
    -ploidy 2 \
    --native-pair-hmm-threads 1 \
    --emit-ref-confidence GVCF

Where:

  • --native-pair-hmm-threads sets the number of threads used by the read-to-haplotype alignment algorithm
  • --emit-ref-confidence determines how likelihoods are emitted for non-variant sites. GVCF makes it score every position, but collapse runs of consecutive sites with comparable confidence into single 'reference blocks''.
The full HaplotypeCaller loop - just for reference 
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Samples are read from a file, one name per line.
IN_FILE=$1
readarray -t SAMPLES < "$IN_FILE"

# The reference and its dictionary are the same for every sample.
REF=./ref/chrom1_1Mb.fa
samtools dict $REF -o ${REF%.fa}.dict

GVCF_DIR=./3.calls/gatk
mkdir -p $GVCF_DIR $GVCF_DIR/logs

for SAMPLE in ${SAMPLES[@]}; do
    echo "Starting sample ${SAMPLE}..."

    BAM=./2.aligned/${SAMPLE}.bam
    GVCF=${GVCF_DIR}/${SAMPLE}.g.vcf.gz
    LOG=${GVCF_DIR}/logs/${SAMPLE}.log

    samtools index $BAM

    # The & at the end sends this into the background, so the loop
    # starts the next sample instead of waiting. Each caller writes to
    # its own log - otherwise the messages of all samples would interleave.
    (
        gatk HaplotypeCaller \
            --java-options "-Xmx4000m" \
            -R $REF \
            -I $BAM \
            -O $GVCF \
            -ploidy 2 \
            --native-pair-hmm-threads 1 \
            --emit-ref-confidence GVCF \
            > $LOG 2>&1
        echo "Finished sample ${SAMPLE}."
    ) &
done

# Without this, the script would exit while the callers are still running.
wait
echo "All samples done."

GATK

Examine the gVCF yourself and try spotting the differences from a regular VCF!

Oof, HaplotypeCaller did not run instantaneously - as expected - but remember this is done only once per sample. Let's copy over all the pre-computed gVCFs...

GVCF_DIR=./3.calls/gatk
# This copies both .g.vcf.gz and .g.vcf.gz.tbi index files
cp /home/Share/reads2snps/3.calls/gatk/*.g.vcf.gz* $GVCF_DIR

...and combine them into one:

# CombineGVCFs inputs
# Rather than 11 arguments, we pass a file listing the gVCFs.
# The grep excludes our own output, in case you run this twice.
GVCF_DIR=./3.calls/gatk
ls $GVCF_DIR/*.g.vcf.gz | grep -v "/littorina" | sort > gvcf.list

# CombineGVCFs outputs
REF=./ref/chrom1_1Mb.fa
GVCF_TMP=./3.calls/gatk/littorina.TMP.g.vcf.gz

# Commands
gatk CombineGVCFs \
   -R $REF \
   --variant gvcf.list \
   -O $GVCF_TMP

Finally, we are ready to perform joint calling:

# GenotypeGVCFs outputs
VCF_FINAL=./3.calls/gatk/littorina.gatk.vcf.gz

# Commands
# GenotypeGVCFs needs a directory for writing intermediate files;
# on a typical computer cluster, this would be /home/scratch or similar.
mkdir ./tmp
time gatk GenotypeGVCFs \
    --java-options "-Xmx4000m" \
    -R $REF \
    --heterozygosity 0.005 \
    --include-non-variant-sites \
    -V $GVCF_TMP \
    -O $VCF_FINAL \
    --tmp-dir ./tmp

# The combined gVCF and the temporary directory are no longer needed
rm ${GVCF_TMP}*
rm -r ./tmp
Where the --heterozygosity value feeds into computing the prior probability that a locus is non-reference (across all samples). Following a state-of-the-art variant calling pipeline tailored to non-model organisms, we set a value that is five-fold higher than the default of 0.001 calibrated for human populations. You can read more on the --heterozygosity flag here.

More on GATK

In a real pipeline, you'd probably prefer GenomicsDBImport over CombineGVCFs (see GATK best practices). The former produces a 'GenomicsDB workspace' rather than a single combined gVCF, which scales far better as samples accumulate.

docs.title: (1.3.7) BONUS: comparing BCFtools and GATK callsets
docs.text:
Now, we have two VCF files to compare: littorina.vcf.gz under 3.calls/bcftools and littorina.gatk.vcf.gz under 3.calls/gatk. If you're curious and have the time and energy, try to work through the following questions:

  1. Which VCF contains more variant sites?

    Show answer 
    VCF_B=3.calls/bcftools/littorina.vcf.gz
VCF_G=3.calls/gatk/littorina.gatk.vcf.gz

# The bcftools manual tells us that -V can be use to EXCLUDE categories of sites
# such as snps, indel or 'ref'. The latter are basically invariant sites!       
bcftools view -H -V ref $VCF_B | wc -l 
bcftools view -H -V ref $VCF_G | wc -l 

# Seems there are so many more invariant sites in the GATK VCF! But is this real?
# Let's check what SITE CATEGORIES there are in the two VCFs
bcftools query -f '%TYPE' $VCF_B | sort | uniq
bcftools query -f '%TYPE' $VCF_G | sort | uniq

# The bcftools VCF ones look standard, but what are all these GATK categories??
# Maybe let's just count 'standard' variant sites...
bcftools view -H -v snps,indels $VCF_G | wc -l

# This looks closer the bcftools number!
# And the other GATK sites? Let's take a look.
bcftools view -H -V snps,indels,ref $VCF_G | less -S
# Maybe at a specific region...
bcftools view -H -r NC_090245.1:118-125 $VCF_G | less -S

# What do you think is going on?

  2. Which VCF contains more indels?

    Show answer 
    bcftools view -H -v indels $VCF_B | wc -l
bcftools view -H -v indels $VCF_G | wc -l
    1. How many SNP sites agree between the two VCFs?
    Show answer 
    # Option 1: this matches both positions & alleles
bcftools isec -n=2 -i 'TYPE="snp"' -i 'TYPE="snp"' $VCF_B $VCF_G | wc -l

# Option 2: this matches positions only
# Why is 'sort' needed here? 🤔 
comm -12 \
    <(bcftools query -i 'TYPE="snp"' -f '%CHROM\t%POS\n' $VCF_B | sort) \
    <(bcftools query -i 'TYPE="snp"' -f '%CHROM\t%POS\n' $VCF_G | sort) | 
    wc -l

docs.title: 1.4. Variant filtering
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this worksheet, you will:

  • Understand the principles of hard and soft filtering.
  • Filter variants with BCFtools.

One could think that a VCF output by a caller represents a final, and indisputable, set of variants. Nothing could be further from the truth! In fact, variant calling is just the first step that is then followed by several stages of variant filtering. Variant filtering is an art - some would say, a dark art - and the best approach depends on your chosen caller software, your dataset, and the purpose of your analysis. While a single 'correct approach' to variant calling almost never exists, it is good practice to make choices that are justified by the sequencing design and features of the data.

docs.title: (1.4.1) Hard filters
docs.text:
There are two ways we can apply filters to genomic data. The most aggressive way is hard filtering, where entire sites are removed from a VCF. For example, some sites might be positioned in genomic regions that are biologically or technically problematic. Similarly, some categories of sites, such as indels or multi-allelic SNPs, might simply fall outside the scope of your intended analysis.

Note that different callers emit different sets of per-site and per-sample annotations (remember the INFO and FORMAT columns?). Annotations are precisely what we're going to use for filtering. Take another look at the header entries of the BCFtools-produced VCF (use bcftools view + grep "##INFO"). Consulting these and, of course, vcf format specs, are the first steps when prepping for variant filtering.

Now, onto the filtering!

Do not overwrite the original VCF

You may ultimately want to filter your original variants in different ways, so do not delete the original VCF! Calling a large dataset can take months (and emit lots of carbon), you do not want to have to repeat it.

docs.title: Step 1: Removing sites by category
docs.text:
Most population genetic analyses are performed on bialellic SNPs only, in line with the assumptions of the infinite sites model. As the first filtering step, we will use a combination of bcftools filter and view to retain biallelic SNPs and invariant sites only:

bcftools filter -Ou -g 5:indel,other ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz | bcftools view -Oz -M 2 -V indels,other,mnps -o ${VCF_PREFIX}.step1.vcf.gz

As always, let's break down the commands.

bcftools filter:

  • -Ou sends an uncompressed VCF through the pipe
  • -g 5:indel,other removes SNPs within 5 bp of an indel or complex variant. Read mismapping around indels tends to generate artefactual SNPs.

bcftools view:

  • -Oz specifies a compressed VCF output.
  • -M 2 retains sites with at most two alleles.
  • -V indels,other,mnps removes every variant that's not a biallelic SNP.

We can immediately inspect how many sites were removed. While, in general, it's a good idea to produce bcftools stats reports at subsequent filtering steps, here we can get away with a more direct bcftools view command:

# Print numbers to screen
bcftools view -H ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz | wc -l
bcftools view -H ${VCF_PREFIX}.step1.vcf.gz | wc -l

# Do some bash arithmetics - just for fun!
N_BEFORE=$(bcftools view -H ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz | wc -l)
echo $N_BEFORE
N_AFTER=$(bcftools view -H ${VCF_PREFIX}.step1.vcf.gz | wc -l)
echo $N_AFTER
awk -v b=$N_BEFORE -v a=$N_AFTER 'BEGIN{printf "Removed: %d sites (%.2f%%)\n", b-a, 100*(b-a)/b}'

You might notice that the unfiltered VCF has >1,000,000 records. This is because some indels cover SNPs, and these are recorded separately.

Just as well, we might wrap the bcftools view commands, and the calculation, in a shell function. We will be able to reuse it later: 

# Shell function
report_removed() {
    local n_before=$(bcftools view -H "$1" | wc -l)
    local n_after=$(bcftools view -H "$2" | wc -l)
    awk -v b="$n_before" -v a="$n_after" \
        'BEGIN{printf "Before: %d\nAfter:  %d\nRemoved: %d sites (%.2f%%)\n", b, a, b-a, 100*(b-a)/b}'
}

# Try it!!
# Arguments are (before, after)
report_removed ${VCF_PREFIX}.vcf.gz ${VCF_PREFIX}.step1.vcf.gz

docs.title: Extracting and visualising fields
docs.text:
Having dropped sites that we don't want to include in the analysis, we can explore variation in the properties of the target sites. We can use bcftools query to extract annotations in a tabular format for further inspection and analysis.

VCF_PREFIX=./3.calls/bcftools/littorina
OUT_DIR=./3.calls/bcftools/pre_filter
mkdir -p $OUT_DIR

bcftools query -f '%DP\n' "${VCF_PREFIX}.step1.vcf.gz" > "${OUT_DIR}/DP_total.txt"
bcftools query -f '%MQ\n' "${VCF_PREFIX}.step1.vcf.gz" > "${OUT_DIR}/MQ.txt"
bcftools query -f '%QUAL\n' "${VCF_PREFIX}.step1.vcf.gz" > "${OUT_DIR}/QUAL.txt"
bcftools query -f '[%DP\t]\n' "${VCF_PREFIX}.step1.vcf.gz" > "${OUT_DIR}/DP_sample.txt"
bcftools query -f '[%GQ\t]\n' "${VCF_PREFIX}.step1.vcf.gz" > "${OUT_DIR}/GQ_sample.txt"
bcftools query -f '[%SP\t]\n' "${VCF_PREFIX}.step1.vcf.gz" > "${OUT_DIR}/SP_sample.txt"

As a reminder - -f reads a string that requests specific fields, % marks a field, square brackets loop over sample-level values, and \t and \n are read literally as tab and new line, respectively. The following annotations are being extracted:

  • DP is the total sequencing depth at a site or per sample, depending on the type of request (i.e., with or without []).
  • MQ is the (arithmetic) mean of Phred-scaled read mapping qualities at a site.
  • QUAL is a Phred-scaled measure of confidence in the call made in the ALT column, whether variant or invariant. For example, a QUAL score of 30 corresponds to a 0.1% probability that the site has been called incorrectly.
  • GQ is the genotype quality (this is only defined per sample)
  • SP is a Phred-scaled p-value that one DNA strand is sequenced at a higher frequency than the other (higher SP = lower p-values). This is generally referred to as strand bias (also only defined per sample).

Look at some of the output files; for example, compare QUAL.txt, DP_sample.txt and GQ_sample.txt. Make sure you understand how (and why) they differ.

To fully appreciate the extent of variation among the annotations of target sites, it's best to do some plotting. To save time today, we provide an R script in the box below. You can save it locally and transfer to the remote machine (call it plot_scores.R) or open a new file on the remote machine using nano (nano plot_scores.R), then paste the contents. The script can be executed as Rscript plot_scores.R. Finally, for plotting, you have two options. You can either (1) produce the plot on the remote machine, and download it for local viewing or (2) download the text files to your machine and do the plotting in your local R Studio.

Plotting script

Note that most annotations are plotted across the full range of values, except SP, for which only non-0 mean per-site values are plotted. 

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)

target <- "./3.calls/bcftools/pre_filter"
files <- c("DP_total.txt", "DP_sample.txt", "QUAL.txt", "MQ.txt", "GQ_sample.txt", "SP_sample.txt")

# Values outside these ranges are treated as missing (files not listed keep all values).
keep_range <- list("SP_sample.txt" = c(1, 50))

read_scores <- function(file, keep = NULL) {
m <- read_table(file, col_names = FALSE, na = ".",
                show_col_types = FALSE) |> as.matrix()
# (0) optionally treat values outside a range as missing. For SP, a zero means
#     "no evidence of strand bias" rather than a measurement, and a handful of
#     extreme outliers otherwise compress the rest of the distribution.
if (!is.null(keep)) m[m < keep[1] | m > keep[2]] <- NA
# (1) drop sites where every sample is missing
m <- m[rowSums(!is.na(m)) > 0, , drop = FALSE]
# (2) mean across samples (columns), if necessary
rowMeans(m, na.rm = TRUE)
}

### Print useful info

# On DP_total
# dpt <- read_scores(file.path(target, "DP_total.txt"))
# dpt_mean <- mean(dpt, na.rm = TRUE)
# cat(sprintf("Mean DP_total is %s\n", dpt_mean))
# cat(sprintf("Mean DP_total x 2.5 is %s\n", dpt_mean * 2.5))
# dpt_high_prop <- sum(dpt > dpt_mean * 2.5) / length(dpt)
# cat(sprintf("This value is exceeded by %.2f%% of sites\n", dpt_high_prop * 100))

### Plot
scores <- files |>
set_names(\(f) tools::file_path_sans_ext(f)) |>
map(\(f) read_scores(file.path(target, f), keep = keep_range[[f]])) |>
map(\(v) tibble(score = v)) |>
list_rbind(names_to = "metric") |>
mutate(metric = factor(metric, levels = tools::file_path_sans_ext(files)))

p <- ggplot(scores, aes(x = score)) +
geom_density(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.8) +
facet_wrap(~ metric, nrow = 2, scales = "free") +
labs(x = "score", y = "density") +
theme_bw()

ggsave(file.path(target, "scores_pre.png"), p, width = 12, height = 6, dpi = 150)

Eye-ball the distributions and make sure that you understand what the axes show. What factors, do you think, dictate the shapes of the curves?

Do it your way!

As it's often the case in bioinformatics, a certain task can be approached in a multitude of ways. For instance, one could like to perform all the procedures outlined here - from VCF parsing to filtering - entirely in R or Python. Specialised libraries exist to help you with that (e.g., vcfR, scikit-allel, sgkit), and the ultimate choice should depend on your comfort, and on what fits best fits your workflows.

docs.title: Step 2: Hard filtering by sequencing depth
docs.text:
The samples we're working with here were sequenced to a depth of approx. 15×. Sequencing and read sampling are partly stochastic processes, however. By necessity, per-site coverage will vary, as we've seen in the plot produced by samtools coverage. On the other hand, sites with exceptionally high depth may represent repetitive sequences or collapsed, duplicated regions of the reference genome. Reads originating from several genomic loci can therefore map to the same position, creating artefactual but high-confidence variant sites...

In general, you should worry more about excessive depth than about low depth: while a shallow site is primarily less informative, a deep site can be actively misleading. Accordingly, we will remove sites where the depth exceeds 2.5 × the mean INFO/DP. If the data was normally distributed, this threshold would demark clear outliers. To compute this threshold, find and uncomment a chunk of code in the plotting script (or unfold the box below).

2.5 × the mean INFO/DP 
DP_MAX=540

Let's apply the INFO/DP filter:

# DP_MAX=
bcftools filter -Oz -e "INFO/DP>${DP_MAX}" ${VCF_PREFIX}.step1.vcf.gz -o ${VCF_PREFIX}.step2.vcf.gz

Here, -e "INFO/DP>${DP_MAX}" excludes sites where the total depth (INFO/DP) is greater than DP_MAX. We can use our shell function to check how many sites were removed:

report_removed ${VCF_PREFIX}.step1.vcf.gz ${VCF_PREFIX}.step2.vcf.gz

Lower INFO/DP threshold

In most cases, there's no need to set a lower threshold on INFO/DP. The reason is that downstream filtering drops uninformative low-DP sites anyway: first, at the QUAL filtering stage, second, when we mask genotypes below a INFO/DP (see below).

docs.title: Steps 3-5: Hard filtering by Phred-scaled scores
docs.text:
We will now filter by three Phred-scaled scores: QUAL, MQ and SP (see above for the definitions). Since these are measures of confidence, any threshold is somewhat arbitrary - are we satisfied with a 0.1% chance of error, or do we insist on 0.01%? Some conventions are nonetheless commonly followed: 30 is a typical choice for QUAL and 40 for MQ.

SP is a slightly different case. First, it is the only one of the three defined per sample rather than per site. Filtering by SP, as applied below, drops sites where the threshold is exceeded for any of the samples. Second, there is no conventional SP threshold - which might be a good opportunity to derive it ourselves, from the plot. What value, do you think, makes sense?

SP threshold

On the one hand, the distribution of mean SP values is bimodal, with one mode around SP = 3 and another around SP = 7. On the other, the distribution appears discretised, with a series of peaks and troughs. Taken together, we decide on SP = 10 - one that encompasses both modes but drops the right-hand tail.

In truth, given SP is a Phred-scaled p-value, one could try to derive the threshold from a significance level, such as the conventional p = 0.05. Using the \(Q = -10\log_{10}p\) formula from the first worksheet, we find that such SP ≈ 13. Not far from our 'informed guess'!

bcftools filter -Oz -e "QUAL<30" ${VCF_PREFIX}.step2.vcf.gz -o ${VCF_PREFIX}.step3.vcf.gz
report_removed ${VCF_PREFIX}.step2.vcf.gz ${VCF_PREFIX}.step3.vcf.gz

bcftools filter -Oz -e "MQ<40" ${VCF_PREFIX}.step3.vcf.gz -o ${VCF_PREFIX}.step4.vcf.gz
report_removed ${VCF_PREFIX}.step3.vcf.gz ${VCF_PREFIX}.step4.vcf.gz

SP_MIN=10
bcftools filter -Oz -e "SP>${SP_MIN}" ${VCF_PREFIX}.step4.vcf.gz -o ${VCF_PREFIX}.step5.vcf.gz
report_removed ${VCF_PREFIX}.step4.vcf.gz ${VCF_PREFIX}.step5.vcf.gz

Generate plots

Ideally, we would like to generate distribution plots after every filtering step. We only skip this due to time constraints.

docs.title: (1.4.2) Soft filtering of genotypes
docs.text:
While hard filtering removes entire sites, we apply soft filtering to mask the genotypes in particualar samples. Masked genotypes are set to missing (./.), as specified by -S .:

bcftools filter -Ou -S . -e "FORMAT/GQ<20" ${VCF_PREFIX}.step5.vcf.gz | bcftools filter -Oz -S . -e 'FORMAT/DP<5' -o ${VCF_PREFIX}.step6.vcf.gz

Above, we apply two kinds of genotype filters. Note how, in both cases, we specify that the annotation comes from the FORMAT column, for a clear distinction. With -e "FORMAT/GQ<20", we mask genotypes with a Phred-scaled quality score below 20 (also a conventional threshold). With -e 'FORMAT/DP<5', we mask genotypes supported by fewer than 5 reads - in which we cannot have any confidence. Think of trying to determine if a coin is biased from just 5 flips!

So, how many sites were removed? ;) 

report_removed ${VCF_PREFIX}.step5.vcf.gz ${VCF_PREFIX}.step6.vcf.gz

Soft filtering definition

Soft filtering is generally defined as any filtering that marks sites or genotypes rather than removing them. At site level, the marks are stored in the FILTER column - which is what bcftools filter -s writes to, whereas the -S above marks genotypes instead.

docs.title: (1.4.3) Missingness filter
docs.text:
As a final site-level filter, we remove sites with a high proportion of missing genotypes. This will account for two sources of missingness. Some sites were not called in the first place, for example, due to lack of coverage. Second, we have just applied genotype-level soft filters. As preparation, we need to calculate one additional annotation, the fraction of missing genotypes F_MISSING:

bcftools +fill-tags ${VCF_PREFIX}.step6.vcf.gz -Oz -o ${VCF_PREFIX}.step7.vcf.gz -- -t F_MISSING

Where:

  • +fill-tags invokes a plugin rather than a built-in command. Plugins extend BCFtools with extra functionality, and are always called with a + prefix.
  • -- separates the options passed to BCFtools itself (before) from those passed to the plugin (after).
  • -t requests F_MISSING to be calculated and added to the INFO column.

We can now filter out sites with more than 10% missing data. In our case, this translates to sites where more than one genotype (1 / 11 ≈ 0.9) are missing. 

bcftools filter -Oz -e "F_MISSING>0.1" ${VCF_PREFIX}.step7.vcf.gz -o ${VCF_PREFIX}.final.vcf.gz

report_removed ${VCF_PREFIX}.step7.vcf.gz ${VCF_PREFIX}.final.vcf.gz

Congratulations - we are done with filtering for today! How many of the original VCF records have we retained? Remember, while our filtering steps are quite standard and could easily 'pass' in a peer-review publication, our primary intention is to give you a flavour of your workflow could look like, rather than provide ready-made solutions. To support your own informed choices, some useful further readings can be found here, here and here.

docs.title: (1.4.4) Replot the distributions
docs.text:
After all the filtering, it's always good to re-visualise the distribution of annotation values. Use the commands below and modify your R script accordingly:

VCF_PREFIX=./3.calls/bcftools/littorina
OUT_DIR=./3.calls/bcftools/post_filter
mkdir -p $OUT_DIR

bcftools query -f '%DP\n' "${VCF_PREFIX}.final.vcf.gz" > "${OUT_DIR}/DP_total.txt"
bcftools query -f '%MQ\n' "${VCF_PREFIX}.final.vcf.gz" > "${OUT_DIR}/MQ.txt"
bcftools query -f '%QUAL\n' "${VCF_PREFIX}.final.vcf.gz" > "${OUT_DIR}/QUAL.txt"
bcftools query -f '[%DP\t]\n' "${VCF_PREFIX}.final.vcf.gz" > "${OUT_DIR}/DP_sample.txt"
bcftools query -f '[%GQ\t]\n' "${VCF_PREFIX}.final.vcf.gz" > "${OUT_DIR}/GQ_sample.txt"
bcftools query -f '[%SP\t]\n' "${VCF_PREFIX}.final.vcf.gz" > "${OUT_DIR}/SP_sample.txt"

docs.title: Principal component analysis (PCA)
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this tutorial, you should be able to

  • Convert a VCF file into PLINK format.
  • Filter variants for linkage disequilibrium before PCA.
  • Perform principal component analysis using PLINK.
  • Understand the difference between eigenvectors and eigenvalues.
  • Plot the major axes of genetic variation.
  • Interpret broad patterns of population structure.
  • Subset individuals and repeat PCA to investigate finer-scale genetic structure.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
Principal component analysis (PCA) is a widely used method for summarising patterns of genetic variation among individuals.

Genomic datasets may contain hundreds of thousands or millions of variable sites. PCA reduces this high-dimensional dataset to a much smaller number of axes, called principal components (PCs).

Each principal component describes an independent axis of variation among individuals. The first principal component explains the greatest amount of variation in the dataset, the second explains the greatest amount of the remaining variation, and so on.

In population genetic datasets, PCA is commonly used to identify: - broad-scale population structure; - genetic differentiation among sampling locations or populations; - clusters of genetically similar individuals; - admixed or intermediate individuals; v finer-scale genetic structure within previously identified groups.

In this tutorial, we will begin with a VCF file, convert it to PLINK format, remove variants in strong linkage disequilibrium, perform PCA, and visualise the results.

We will then repeat the PCA using a subset of individuals to investigate finer-scale patterns of genetic variation.

docs.title: 2. The dataset
docs.text:
In this exercise we will work with a dataset that compares patterns of genome-wide variation between egg-laying and live-bearing populations from the genus Littorina. The dataset of 3 named species: L. saxatilis, L. compressa and L. arcana.

This dataset predates our chromosome-level assembly for Littorina, so includes many small contigs. This version of the dataset includes a subset of 1000 randomly selected contigs to make the analysis more computationally efficient.

Let's start by making a directory called PCA in our root directory (get here using cd ~) using mkdir

Then we need to copy the data to this new directory. You can find it here:

/home/Share/pca/108_littorina_10000contigs.vcf.gz
